objective: Connect the Glasgow surname branches into one extended family tree, developing and testing tentative connections from the earliest records first.
common_origin: The owner reports that all men tested share the Glasgow Y-DNA lineage. A shared paternal origin around 1400–1450, possibly earlier, is the working research model; the founder, date and intervening generations remain to be identified.
later_records: Use records after 1850 when they can resolve an earlier identity, migration or branch connection; routine descendant reconstruction is secondary.

metrics.family_heads: Male surname bearers without a father in the selected pedigree and with at least two surname-bearing children; also queue heads with at least two descendants through one child.
metrics.components: Separate paternal components, including isolated surname bearers. Mothers, spouses and marriage connections cannot join surname branches.
metrics.largest_component: Percentage of the selected historical surname cohort in its largest paternal component.
metrics.confidence: Show confidently marked links and the working pedigree separately. Existing tree grades are not a claim that every underlying record has been independently audited.
metrics.baseline: Preserve the initial cohort IDs and input fingerprint. Compare the same surviving baseline people as well as current totals; report additions and missing people separately. Do not improve the score with a virtual founder, invented parent or incompatible alternative fathers.
metrics.target: One connected paternal component and 100% connected pairs in the working pedigree; a complete pedigree can retain one earliest family head. Keep the strongly assessed result separate.

early_connections.basis: Glasgow-2462 is the proposed, very uncertain working father of the traditional Ulster ancestor Glasgow-591 and the Cavers Covenanter Glasgow-4138. This carries the existing possible identity with the Polwarth child Glasgow-1605 into a concrete local family model. The Polwarth index names the child’s father as William Glasgow, and Glasgow-2462 is already attached to that child with uncertainty. The three younger profile accounts are retained as possible stages of one life, not three proved brothers. Neither new father attachment is independent support for the other: both depend on the same child/adult identity and on the unproved identification of the named Polwarth father with the Inveresk man. The Polwarth child was baptised on 4 April 1658. If baptised near birth, he would have been about 21 at the examination of the Cavers servant in June 1679, 26 at the Ormistoun servant list in 1684 and 31 in 1689. Those are compatible ages for the recorded adult and the later military tradition. The Ulster profile’s circa 1656 birth is explicitly a rough grandson-based estimate, not an age stated by a record; its guessed Glasgow-city origin cannot exclude a Borders childhood. The exact forename and surname, compatible sequence and existing Borders candidate make this a usable provisional life model. Polwarth and Cavers are distinct parishes in different counties, and the chronology supplies compatibility rather than an identifying age match. The Cavers setting is recorded residence/association, not a proved birthplace. The Cavers man is the leading existing Scottish comparison for Glasgow-591 because the records establish a Covenanter and wreck survivor before the reported 1689 episode, while a probable member of his actual parish survivor group, James Young, appears among survivors said to have reached Ulster. Waddell’s 1886 account says all fifty survivors reached northern Ireland; his revised 1902 account says only some and omits both Glasgows from its named list. The omission does not exclude William, but the revision and late publication weaken the blanket migration claim. The 1684 Ormistoun record also prevents assuming uninterrupted Ulster residence from 1679. The later family history’s 1689 service and settlement remain tradition, not verified military service. No particular crossing, return journey, unit or Irish residence is invented. Its Cameron-to-Glasgow surname-origin story cannot explain a man already called Glasgow in 1679. The weakest stage is the proposed father’s identity. Glasgow-2462 was born at Inveresk on 20 August 1639 and baptised the next day. He would have been only 18 at the 1658 Polwarth baptism and 16, nearly 17, at the associated Elizabeth baptism in August 1656. Young fatherhood is possible, but there is no marriage, residence or occupation connecting him with the named Polwarth father. An older, otherwise unidentified William is a substantial competing explanation. The named-child clause does not prove Glasgow-2462’s identity. The regional Polwarth/Gordon household of Glasgow-3107 is a stronger local kinship lead than Inveresk alone, but supplies no father clause for William; no exact brother, uncle or father relationship with James is selected. This inherited father remains a very low-confidence default and would fall away on both new adult accounts if the child/father identification fails. No mother is selected for either adult, and no wife or mother is transferred from the Inveresk ancestry. The Polwarth child could be a different man from the Cavers Covenanter, and the Covenanter could be different from the late family history’s William. The Hawick father Glasgow-2731 in 1692 and Cavers groom Glasgow-3587 in 1708/09 remain competing later identities for the Covenanter; neither is newly equated with him. The attached Glasgow-3370 entry in 1694 does not independently establish the Polwarth man as her father. If later Scottish records identify the Covenanter continuously there, the family history’s permanent Irish settlement would need reconsideration. Other Scottish William candidates and the possibility that the late ancestor account is mistaken remain open. A missing contemporary Irish bridge is not an exclusion, but the combined identification is especially uncertain. No surname or Y-DNA grouping supplies these missing generations. Two very uncertain local father hypotheses are selected from existing research; no new original inspection, certain relationship, identity merge or live WikiTree save. Existing child/adult records, vital fields, attached relatives and their grades remain unchanged. Connectivity counts retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates, and describes the selected model rather than a proved pedigree.
early_connections.next_test: Test the named Polwarth father against the Inveresk child, the Polwarth child against the Cavers adult and the Cavers adult against the late Irish ancestor account; retain all three separate uncertainty boundaries.

early_connections.title: Larne and Inishrush: James’s possible sons Adam and Alexander
early_connections.status: Two selected uncertain fathers; possible brother route; no mother selected

people.name: Older Alexander Glasgow, reconstructed Bann Valley father

early_connections.basis: Glasgow-1509, the older Larne ropemaker, is selected as the uncertain working father of Adam of Inishrush (Glasgow-3902). This adopts the named-family comparison already tested in September. Adam’s gravestone age implies birth about 1758; James’s reported 1737 birth would give an ordinary age-21 generation. The original 1773 affidavit independently places the Larne James’s birth before October 1743, although it does not prove the reported 1737 year. Adam’s proved son James (Glasgow-3903) supplies limited positive naming support. James is a documented adult with a trade and property trail, making him a more useful provisional father than the recordless Glasgow-3905 placeholder. No record names Adam as his child, and the naming argument is weak rather than corroboration of a parent clause. The same James is selected, with very low confidence, as father of the reconstructed older Alexander (Glasgow-3904). This adopts the existing possible-brother route for Adam and Alexander. On the reported 1737 and estimated 1770 years, James would be about 33 at Alexander’s birth. Making Adam, born about 1758, Alexander’s father instead produces a twelve-year interval. Alexander’s circa 1770 birth is only an estimate, so that calculation does not exclude an Adam father: Alexander could have been born later. However, fatherhood of Daniel by about 1795/96 places Alexander in a generation born by roughly 1775–1778, leaving two short successive generations in the Adam-to-Alexander model. Adam’s wife Unknown-760890, born about 1766/67 from her monument age, cannot be Alexander’s mother on that chronology. The sibling route is therefore preferred provisionally without inventing an earlier wife. Chronological economy does not prove brotherhood or a shared father; neither selected edge is independent support for the other. A 1760 lease identifies James as a Belfast ropemaker taking a ropewalk at Gardenmore, Larne; the 1768 assignment identifies the same property. This is a real occupational and locality sequence, distinct from the contemporary Larne tanner. Adam is documented much later at Inishrush, and the monument does not state his birthplace. The estimated Inishrush birth cannot exclude a family from elsewhere, but no Belfast birth or Larne-to-Inishrush migration is newly assigned. The 1773 Larne gentleman’s age excludes the younger Glasgow-3991 account; the identity assessment and separation of the two trades retain their previous grades. The reported James/Shutter-46 marriage in 1762 is later than Adam’s birth. It cannot establish Shutter-46 as Adam’s mother. An earlier union, premarital birth or inaccurate reported date would be needed if this father model is right; no such event or person is invented. Shutter-46 is not selected as older Alexander’s mother either: the marriage report and the son identity are independently unproved. The two local 1740 Tamlaght Hugh households, including Glasgow-3931, and the older Adam-and-Maria naming model remain alternatives for Adam. A different unrecorded father remains possible. Neither Larne property succession nor the Inishrush household totals connect these generations. The 1831 return does not identify its unnamed occupants, and the later plot-29 succession is not evidence of James the ropemaker’s paternity. The shared Glasgow-3905 field is a recently created research placeholder, not evidence that Adam, older Alexander and Glasgow-1367 were brothers. It is not identified or merged with James. No father is extended to Glasgow-1367, and no unnamed extra generation is added. Older Alexander is himself reconstructed chiefly from late descendant testimony naming Thomas’s parents as Alexander and Rosanna. The 2007 account and its copied 2020 restatement are one source tradition, not independent witnesses. Daniel and Thomas are proved brothers, but their father’s name is not established by a contemporary parent record. The new James father therefore depends on that reconstructed older Alexander account. Younger Glasgow-951 remains a separate, unresolved possible brother or cousin of Thomas and Daniel; the record-defined Glasgow-4090 remains his leading current father comparison. This batch does not select older Alexander as younger Alexander’s father or place that younger family beneath James. No Rosanna surname or October 1822 death date is newly established. James’s own Glasgow-1505 and Glasgow-1499 ancestry alternatives and existing children retain their earlier assessments. Two named father hypotheses are selected from existing research, with low/very low confidence. No new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save. All existing vital fields and confidently marked metrics remain unchanged. Mothers are independently unassigned. The local model replaces the placeholder father only in these two selected views; captured WikiTree fields and rival parentage remain available. Counts describe retained profile accounts and conditional ancestry, not a proved pedigree.

early_connections.title: West Kilbride and Maryland: a conditional Ayrshire family
early_connections.status: Two selected uncertain fathers through possible childhood identities; no mother selected

people.name: Rev. Patrick Glasgow, Manokin and Snow Hill

early_connections.basis: John Glasgow-3375 is the selected uncertain working father of the West Kilbride parent John Glasgow-3161, through possible identity with his son Jon Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning on 6 July 1679. The West Kilbride account already names Glasgow-1434 as an identity comparison. A child born near the 1679 baptism could have been about twenty at the January 1700 Patrick event, followed by the John/Margaret Cowan children at nearby Stevenston in 1701 and 1706 if that further adult identity is right. This supplies a specific neighbouring-parish household and ordinary generation, preferred provisionally to leaving the 1700 father without a named family. It does not prove that the Kilwinning child, Stevenston father and West Kilbride father were one person. The West Kilbride John Glasgow-3161 is the selected uncertain working father of Rev. Patrick Glasgow-635, through possible identity with the indexed child Patrick Glasgow-3160 of 1700. The minister’s church-history account calls him Patrick, and the previously reviewed biography of his son calls the father a native of Scotland. If the 1700 child became the minister, he would have been about thirty-five when son James was born in 1735, thirty-six when ordained at Manokin in 1736, and fifty-three at his death in 1753. That is a coherent adult career and family sequence. The recorded Scottish childhood and compatible dates make this a useful low-confidence choice; no ministerial, marriage or migration record identifies that child as the Maryland man. The supplied Scotland’s People entry reads PATRICK GLASGOW, 03/01/1700, West Kilbride, parish 620, reference 10 / 27, with JOHN GLASGOW/ as the parent field. The prior source review interprets that as 3 January; the structured child field instead says 1 March. Both readings remain visible, and neither an exact birthday nor original-image inspection is claimed. The minister’s inherited circa-1680 Irish birth is unsupported by his cited career records. Taken literally, 1680 would conflict with this childhood hypothesis and with a father represented by the 1679 Kilwinning child. It remains a conflicting profile estimate, not evidence that the proposed generations fit that year. No date or birthplace is silently changed to make the route work. Scottish origin rests on a later biographical statement, not a contemporary birthplace record. Ford’s church history, printed p.16, PDF p.22, records the 1736–1741 ministry and 23 March 1753 death, but names no parent and supplies no age or birthplace. John Glasgow-551, associated with County Tyrone in the William Melanchthon Glasgow family account, remains an alternative identity already named on the West Kilbride profile. His estimated birth and the absence of a West Kilbride event do not exclude him. The Ayrshire comparison is preferred for its specific neighbouring parishes and independently indexed 1679 child, not because an Irish route has been disproved. Another local John, a brother or cousin of the Kilwinning family, or a different father remains possible. The Kilwinning-child/Stevenston-adult identity is itself uncertain. No occupation, later residence or marriage connects John-3161 to either adult. Barbara Alason/Allason is named with the 1679 child; no mother is selected for the West Kilbride account, and Margaret Cowan is not assigned as Patrick’s mother from the later Stevenston events. John-3375’s earlier family scaffold retains its existing uncertainty. The Gordon Patrick Glasgow-1440, indexed in 1667 and associated with Helen Fairburn and a later Scottish family, remains an alternative childhood/adult comparison. He would have been about sixty-eight at James’s 1735 birth and sixty-nine at the 1736 ordination if baptised near birth: less economical than the 1700 route, but not an exclusion. The Maryland-linked Patrick Glasgow-3002 is another unresolved account; its unsupported 1720 birth estimate does not identify or exclude him as the minister, and its cited Treasury entry has not been newly interpreted here. Other unrecorded Scottish or Irish childhoods remain possible. The 1700 child’s later life and the minister’s pre-1736 life are untraced. Shared forename, surname and plausible ages are indirect evidence, not a parent clause. Mary Jones remains the minister’s recorded wife; no new marriage, mother, migration date or Scottish parish of birth is asserted. Two uncertain father hypotheses are selected; both depend on unproved child/adult identities. Their combination is a conditional model, not two independent confirmations of an Ayrshire-to-Maryland descent. The corresponding child and adult accounts are retained separately without a merge; connectivity counts retained profile accounts rather than proved distinct people. No original parish image, new kinship clause, certain relationship upgrade, mother assignment or live WikiTree save is claimed. Current vital fields and confidently marked relationships are preserved, with the conflicting estimates explicitly explained.

early_connections.title: Carnwath Robert: a conditional Lindsaylands father
early_connections.status: One selected uncertain father; later-weaver identity and earlier Robert birth required

people.name: Johne Glasgow, Mid Calder child of 1648

early_connections.basis: James Glasgow-3332 is the selected uncertain working father of Robert Glasgow-3407, who married Katherine Wilson at Carnwath in 1713 and is associated with son John Glasgow-2870 at Libberton in 1722. This is conditional on James representing the weaver at Back of Lindsaylands whose testament was indexed in 1680. The adjacent Biggar, Libberton and Carnwath family setting supplies a specific local comparison. A James born around the inherited 1630/1634 estimates could father Robert in the 1660s or 1670s; a Robert born in the 1670s could marry in 1713 and father John in 1722 at ordinary adult ages. This provisional older-generation route is preferred to making the two overlapping Libberton Roberts sons of the same Johne. No record names Robert as the weaver’s child. Robert’s current circa-1690 birth estimate would be too late for a father dead by 1680; an earlier birth is required if this hypothesis is right. That estimate is unsupported, but the required revision remains a limitation, not evidence for the proposed father. The 1680 index describes James as a weaver in the Back of Lindsaylands, parish of Biggar, with indexed testament date 10 November 1680, Lanark Commissary Court CC14/5/10, TD. That is a registration date, not an exact death date. The original has not been read and supplies no reviewed Robert clause. The 1690 Edinburgh apprenticeship names a deceased father James Glasgow, weaver in Lindsayland; the matching trade and locality make him a probable instance of the indexed weaver, but identification with Glasgow-3332 remains only possible. The apprentice generation is another possible intermediary for the later family, not an additional person invented to complete a pedigree. James Glasgow-3332’s existing parentage, the separate 1648 Johne child identity, and the competing 1624 Quothquan-weaver identity retain their previous grades. The new father selection cannot itself prove any of those identities or be used circularly to reject the 1624 alternative. This particular parent model depends on the later weaver identity; the 1624 decedent would be an implausibly early direct father of this 1713–1722 household. The Carnwath marriage citation gives Robert and Katherine Wilson in 1713; the captured 1722 Libberton baptism citation names Robert and Katharin Wilson as John’s parents. Those index citations define the proposed Wilson household but supply no paternal ancestry or age for Robert. The neighbouring Robert Glasgow-4168 account combines Katherin Gibson in 1718 and Katherine Watson in 1720 and 1726. The Wilson event in 1722 falls between the Watson events. Consequently, a simple sequence of remarriages does not reconcile all maternal surnames. Transcription differences, record misassignment, overlapping families, or one man across some entries remain possible. No woman is equated with another, and no new marriage or mother is assigned. The two Robert accounts are retained separately; shared parish and forename do not prove identity. Johne Glasgow-3093 remains an unselected alternative father for the Carnwath Robert, particularly if Robert Glasgow-3407 is eventually identified with the Gibson/Watson Robert Glasgow-4168, whose selected father is already Johne. Johne’s birth around 1648 could fit fatherhood around 1690; however, no later record follows him from the Mid Calder child entry to Libberton. Giving him both Roberts would otherwise require two living sons with the same forename or an unproved identity between the accounts. The present choice avoids building that assumption into the default model. If James Glasgow-3332’s two father assignments and the Johne Glasgow-3093 to Robert Glasgow-4168 choice are right, Robert Glasgow-3407 would be the latter Robert’s paternal uncle. That is a consequence of the conditional model, not independent evidence of kinship. Another unrecorded local father and a younger Lindsaylands generation remain possible. Captain Robert Glasgow-2867 also remains a surviving identity comparison; his unsupported imported family is not a concrete exclusion, and no maritime or probate bridge identifies the Carnwath man with him. One new uncertain father is selected from existing index and family reviews. The 1680 weaver identity and an earlier Robert birth are required conditions; no new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, mother assignment, identity merge or live WikiTree save is claimed. Existing vital fields and confidently marked metrics are unchanged. The two Robert accounts remain separate retained profiles, and no genealogical certainty is inferred from their inclusion in one working family.

early_connections.title: Irvine’s 1693 father: a very uncertain Kilwinning childhood
early_connections.status: Very uncertain father and mother through one child/adult identity; fourteen-year age problem explicit

people.name: John Glasgow, proposed Irvine father of 1693

early_connections.basis: John Glasgow-3375 is the selected very uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3018, treating the latter provisionally as the father named with Agnes Martine in the 1693 Irvine child entry. The route adopts the existing comparison with John Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning on 6 July 1679 as child of John and Barbara Alason. Exact forename and surname, the neighbouring Ayrshire parishes, and a specific recorded child/parent pair make this a usable local model. It is not a merge or an identification of all events currently collected under either account. If the 1679 event was an infant baptism, that child would have been only fourteen by the 1693 entry. This is a serious weakness. Baptism of an older child would allow an older father, but no evidence establishes such a baptism; neither an earlier birth nor unusually young fatherhood is asserted as fact. The current circa-1675 birth is an inherited estimate, not independent support for the match. Barbara Allison-6866 is separately selected as the very uncertain working mother through the same proposed 1679-child identity. The indexed 1679 entry actually names Barbara Alason; this is not a mother invented from the father choice or supplied from the surname-only 1689 entry. The existing Allison profile represents that Alason/Allason household and is a compatible account. Her circa-1659 birth is also an estimate, and no date, birthplace or marriage is newly established. The mother identification and the adult John identification remain unproved. These two parent links depend on one child/adult comparison; they are not independent confirmations of the proposed family. The Irvine source is the supplied Scotland’s People OPR index: JOHN GLASGOW, 08/10/1693, parish 595, reference 10 / 12, FR23, parents JOHN GLASGOW/AGNES MARTINE. The previous review interprets this as 8 October; the structured child field instead says 10 August 1693. Both readings remain visible, and an index from a combined births/baptisms collection does not establish a birthday. John Glasgow-1473 is retained as the child-record account. Identification with the John Glasgow younger active as skipper in 1720, the 1719 father of Grizal, or the later bursary recipient remains separate and uncertain. Neither the elder/younger wording nor the new grandparents prove those adult identities or an elder skipper’s paternity. Agnes Martine remains the mother named in the 1693 record; no new spouse or parent-field certainty is assigned to the child account. The 1725 elder skipper, 1729 Sailors’ Poor Box treasurer, 1734 deceased shipmaster and 1740 living bailie are not newly equated with the 1693 father. The 1734 catalogue describes heirs of a late shipmaster, while the 1740 entry names a living merchant/bailie; those occurrences cannot be one man. Glasgow-1077 remains a compatible candidate for the later bailie, independently of this parent model; the recorded 1690 child is not adopted as the 1693 adult father. The new parent fields are scoped to the 1693 father proposition, not an assertion that the composite biography is one proved life. All later occurrences and original archive references remain available without an invented death date or transfer of records between profiles. The same 1679 child remains only possibly identical with the Stevenston father of John in 1701 and Adam in 1706. The alleged two-John-sons conflict does not justify excluding the Irvine match when those identities and the survival of the children are unproved. No intervening death, second baptism or remarriage is invented to reconcile the accounts. The already selected West Kilbride John Glasgow-3161 route also uses this childhood comparison, so it provides no independent corroboration here. The retained adult accounts may be duplicates rather than distinct brothers. An older Irvine John, another local parent, or identification of the 1693 father with the older John Glasgow-3375 rather than his proposed son remain alternatives; the last option would collapse the new father edge as an identity duplicate. The older John’s possible identity with minister Glasgow-1073 and earlier ancestry keep their previous uncertainty; this is not a new proved son of the minister. One father and one mother are selected, both very uncertain and dependent on the same 1679-child/1693-adult identity. This is one new paternal branch connection, not two independent ancestry discoveries. No original parish image, new contemporary kinship clause, certainty upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save is claimed. Vital fields, existing parent grades and the separate later adult identities are preserved. Connectivity counts retained profile accounts, including possible duplicates, rather than proved distinct people.
